lessons.title: Arch Bridge
lessons.description:
An Arch Bridge carries loads using a curved structural shape. When weight acts on the bridge, the arch carries forces mainly through compression. Those forces travel along the curve toward the supports at both ends.

The end supports are called Abutments. They must resist the outward thrust, or push, produced by the arch. How the arch connects to these supports is important to the crossing.

A curved structure can help leave space beneath the roadway. The bridge must still provide sufficient clearance for the traffic or waterway below it. In Marsh's project, taxis and residents need a safe route above while boats need enough room to pass beneath.

During testing, observe how the arch and its supports respond as the vehicle crosses. Then check whether the boat can pass safely beneath the bridge. A successful crossing must support the traffic above without blocking the waterway below.

lessons.title: BEAM BRIDGE
lessons.description: A beam bridge is a structural system consisting primarily of horizontal beams supported by piers, columns, or abutments. When a downward load acts on the bridge, the beam bends, generally producing compression on one side and tension on the other. These forces are carried through the structure toward its supports. Beam bridges are commonly suited to relatively short spans because increasing the distance between supports increases the structural demands on the beam.

lessons.title: Bending
lessons.description:
Bending is the curving or deformation of a structural member under an applied load. When a vehicle crosses a bridge, its weight creates a downward load. The connected structural members carry this load toward the supports.

For a simply supported bridge with a load at midspan, the greatest bending moment commonly occurs near the middle. The position and amount of bending depend on the load position, supports, and structural arrangement.

When a simply supported beam bends downward under a vehicle's weight, its upper part experiences compression, while its lower part experiences tension. Compression pushes material together; tension pulls it apart.

Understanding bending helps you identify areas that may need additional structural support. Proper material choices, connected members, and support arrangements help a bridge withstand bending safely.

During Reed's factory crossing test, observe how the bridge responds as the pickup moves across. Watch for members that curve or deform most under the load, then review whether the design needs more support.

lessons.title: What is Compression
lessons.description:
Compression is a pushing force that squeezes or shortens a structural member.
When a member is under compression, forces push toward each other from opposite ends. If the compression becomes too great, the member may crush, bend, or buckle.
Columns, piers, and bridge supports commonly resist compression.
Bridge Example:
Bridge piers experience compression as they carry the weight of the bridge and transfer it to the ground.

lessons.title: Dead Load
lessons.description: A dead load is the load associated with the permanent components of a structure. For a bridge, this includes the self-weight of structural components such as the deck, beams, trusses, piers, barriers, and other permanently attached elements. Unlike live loads, these loads generally remain in place and continuously act on the structure throughout its service life.

lessons.title: What is Equilibrium
lessons.description:
Structural Equilibrium is the condition in which the forces and moments acting on a structure are balanced. Both force balance and moment balance are needed for a stationary bridge.

The weight of the bridge and a crossing vehicle act downward. The supports provide upward reactions that help balance these loads. As a vehicle changes position, the forces carried by the members and supports change too. If forces or moments are unbalanced, the structure may move or rotate.

Equilibrium alone does not mean a bridge is safe for any load. Its members, connections, and supports must also have enough strength and stability to carry the required loads without failing.

lessons.title: Live Load
lessons.description: A live load is a temporary or variable force imposed on a structure by occupants, vehicles, equipment, materials, or other objects that are not permanently part of the structure. On a bridge, live loads may change in magnitude and position as vehicles or pedestrians move across the deck, causing different structural members to experience changing forces. FHWA guidance, for example, distinguishes temporary construction live loads such as workers, tools, supplies, materials, and equipment from permanent structural loads.

lessons.title: Load Distribution
lessons.description:
Load Distribution refers to how an applied load is shared among the structural members and supports of a bridge. A vehicle's weight does not affect only the section directly beneath it. The connected members work together to carry that load toward the supports.

The bridge's design, connections, support placement, and vehicle position affect how the load is shared. Some members or supports may carry more than others; placing additional supports does not guarantee equal loading. Adding or repositioning a support can change the load carried throughout the structure.

During a moving-load test, observe the entire bridge, including the surrounding members and supports. A response away from the vehicle can still be part of the structure carrying its load. Check that each part can safely withstand the demand placed on it.

For Silas's community crossing, consider the available support points and the lower rock formation when arranging the structure. Choose a connected design that safely carries the test vehicle while distributing its load toward the supports. Test the whole crossing rather than judging only the section immediately below the vehicle.

lessons.title: Load Transfer
lessons.description:
Load Transfer describes how forces travel through connected structural components until they reach the supports, foundations, and eventually the ground. It focuses on the load path; load distribution describes how that load is shared among members and supports.

A vehicle applies its weight to the deck. The deck and its connected components must provide a continuous path that carries those forces toward suitable supports. The path depends on the type of bridge and how its parts are connected.

Example: a suspension bridge
Deck → Hangers → Main Cables → Towers and Anchorages → Ground

In this example, hangers carry load from the deck to the main cables. The cables carry tension, pass over towers, and are secured at anchorages. Towers carry compressive forces toward the ground, while anchor points resist the cables' pull. This is one possible structural arrangement, not a requirement to use the same design on every crossing.

For Silas's eastern passage, rope and the existing wooden towers offer another way to support connected bridge components. Think carefully about their connections and the available anchor points. If you use those supports, make sure they form part of a continuous load path. Every component has a role in carrying and transferring the vehicle's load safely.

lessons.title: Material Stress
lessons.description:
Material Stress is the internal force per unit area developed within a material under load. Loads placed on a bridge create internal stresses in its structural members. These stresses can occur due to tension, compression, bending, or shear.

Different materials can withstand different amounts of stress. Each material has its own strength and allowable stress limits. Concrete, for example, generally handles compression well but is weaker in tension unless it is reinforced.

If the stress in a member exceeds what its material can safely withstand, the member may crack, deform excessively, or fail. Choosing suitable materials and arranging the supports properly helps keep stresses within safe limits under the applied loads.

Ford's loaded cargo trucks carry heavier loads than the taxi from the previous project. During testing, watch how the bridge and its supports respond as a loaded truck moves across. Observe which members experience the greatest stress, and consider whether the supports or structural arrangement need adjustment.

lessons.title: Moving Load
lessons.description:
A Moving Load is a load that changes position along a structure, such as a vehicle traveling across a bridge. Unlike a load that remains in one place, a vehicle applies its weight at different positions as it moves.

The forces and stresses in the bridge can change throughout a crossing. Different vehicle positions can produce different bending moments and support reactions. For a simply supported bridge, the support closest to a vehicle generally carries a greater share of that vehicle's weight when it is near one end. The bending effect near the center generally increases as the vehicle approaches the middle.

A bridge must remain safe from one end of the crossing to the other, not just at the starting point or middle. Testing a vehicle over the entire span lets you observe how the structural response changes with its position.

Brooks's market connection must safely carry both taxis and heavier delivery vehicles. Watch how the bridge responds as each vehicle enters, travels along the span, and approaches the opposite side. Continue observing until each vehicle has completely crossed.

lessons.title: Shear
lessons.description:
Shear is an internal force that acts across a section of a structural member and resists adjacent parts sliding relative to each other. Shear forces develop when loads act on a structure. When a heavy vehicle crosses a bridge beam, its weight acts downward while the supports provide upward reactions.

Shear and bending are different internal effects, but both can occur in the same structural member. In a simply supported beam carrying a load near the middle, shear force is often greatest in the regions near the supports. Its significance depends on the load and how the bridge is supported.

A structural member must safely withstand the shear forces acting on it. Excessive shear can cause cracking or structural failure. Review the members near the supports as well as the safety of the entire bridge.

Ronan's southern connection must carry a heavy vehicle across a 100-meter gap with different road elevations. During testing, observe how the structural members near the supports respond as the vehicle enters, moves along the span, and approaches the opposite side. Continue observing until the vehicle has completed the crossing.

lessons.title: Structural Failure
lessons.description:
Structural Failure occurs when a structure or component can no longer safely resist the applied forces or perform its intended function. A bridge must carry its required load and remain usable.

Where failure begins matters. The first problem may occur in one member or connection, without an immediate collapse of the entire bridge. The remaining members may then have to carry a different share of the load.

In real structures, failure can involve excessive bending, cracking, buckling, connection damage, or loss of stability. A member under compression may buckle; a beam may deform excessively; a connection may be unable to transfer the required forces. Different problems call for different changes.

Movement is not always failure. Some movement under load is normal. Engineers consider whether movement stays within safe limits and whether the structure can continue performing its intended function.

At Mills's Heavy Equipment Route, watch the mobile crane throughout the crossing. If the test fails, identify the first overloaded or broken area, check how its members connect, and improve the load path before testing again. Avoid changing the whole bridge without examining the results.

About this test: the game checks pulling and compression forces against configured member limits and tracks broken parts. It does not separately calculate every real-world bending, shear, twisting, cracking, or connection failure. The lesson describes the broader engineering concept; passing the game test is not a real-world load rating.

lessons.title: Suspension Bridge
lessons.description:
A Suspension Bridge uses main cables supported by towers, with vertical hangers connecting the cables to the roadway. This arrangement can span long distances when the components and their connections safely carry the load.

Hangers transfer loads from the roadway to the main cables. The main cables primarily carry tension. The towers primarily carry compression toward the ground, and the anchorages resist the cables' pulling forces.

A truck puts weight on the roadway as it moves. The roadway, hangers, cables, towers, and anchorages need to stay connected so that their forces can reach the foundations and ground. At Clark's Freight Passage, watch how the load shifts across the span and check those connections if the truck cannot finish the crossing.

lessons.title: What is Tension
lessons.description:
Tension is a pulling force that stretches a structural member.
When a member is under tension, forces pull away from each other at opposite ends. The member becomes slightly longer as it carries the load. If the tension becomes greater than the material’s strength, the member may stretch excessively or break.
Cables, ropes, and the lower portions of some bridge components commonly resist tension.
Bridge Example:
The main cables of a suspension bridge are placed under tension as they support the bridge deck.

lessons.title: Tension & Compression
lessons.description:
Tension is a pulling force that stretches a structural member. Forces pull away from each other at opposite ends of the member. Excessive tension can cause the member to stretch too much or break.

Compression is a pushing force that squeezes or shortens a member. Forces push toward each other from opposite ends. Excessive compression can cause crushing or buckling, depending on the material and shape.

When a vehicle crosses a bridge, the roadway and connected structural members transfer its weight toward the supports. In a truss bridge, some members can carry tension while others carry compression under the same load. The forces in each member depend on the structural arrangement, support positions, and where the vehicle is along the crossing.

Engineers must choose suitable materials and arrange members so they can safely withstand these forces. Understanding tension and compression helps identify which parts need stronger members or a better load path; it does not remove the need to test the bridge.

For Vance's transport crossing, load the cargo onto the vehicle before testing. The cargo adds to the vehicle's load. Watch how the members work together as the loaded vehicle crosses, and check how their responses change as it moves.

lessons.title: Torsion
lessons.description:
Torsion occurs when a moment acts around a structural member's longitudinal axis and tends to twist it. It differs from stretching, compression, or vertical bending.

Off-center loading can create torsion. A vehicle closer to one bridge edge may produce an uneven response across the width. For the same downward force, increasing its sideways distance from the structure's center of resistance increases the twisting moment. The actual response also depends on the bridge's shape, stiffness, connections, and supports.

Engineers consider both the downward load and the twisting moment. Connected members across the deck help distribute loads and resist twisting. Excessive torsion can cause deformation, cracking, or failure. A centered load does not automatically remove every source of torsion.

At Clark's Offset Road, the lane stays closer to one side to work around factory equipment. Consider why that position matters in a real bridge, and keep the roadway and supports connected throughout the SUV crossing.

About this test: this game test checks pulling and compression. Twisting across the bridge width is not measured. The offset lane illustrates the site constraint; passing this crossing does not prove that a real bridge can safely resist torsion.

lessons.title: What is Truss
lessons.description:
A Truss Bridge is a framework of connected structural members arranged in triangular patterns. Loads entering through the roadway travel through these members toward the bridge supports.

Triangular arrangements help the framework maintain its shape when forces act on it. They still require proper connections, suitable supports, and members with enough strength; adding triangles does not make every bridge safe.

In an ideal pin-jointed truss, members mainly carry axial forces: tension pulls and compression pushes along a member. Real members and connections can also experience bending. Later lessons explore these forces in more detail.

materials.name: Wood Beam
materials.description: Wood beams resist pulling (tension) and pushing (compression). Connect them in triangles to carry loads from the roadway to the supports. They are light and inexpensive, making them useful for short truss members. Each placement adds one beam on each side of the deck.

materials.name: Concrete Pier
materials.description: A Concrete Pier carries loads from a bridge joint down to the foundation in compression. It can carry more compression than a Wood Pier of the same height, and it adds more weight and cost. Check tall piers during the test because their compression capacity drops as they get taller.

materials.name: Reinforced Concrete Road Deck
materials.description: A reinforced concrete driving deck with higher tensile capacity than timber roads. Connect it to triangulated beams or supported piers; a flat unsupported deck can still collapse. Its reinforcement carries tension while the concrete carries compression. Heavier and more expensive than wood, with a 10 m placement limit. Mass and strength are balanced gameplay values, not real-world engineering ratings.

materials.name: Concrete Beam
materials.description: Reinforced concrete beams support the Concrete Road deck and transfer its weight and vehicle loads to anchored joints or piers. Use triangular bracing and short supported spans; an unanchored beam cannot support a bridge just by touching it. Each placement creates two side beams, so its price and mass are doubled. Stronger than timber, but heavier and more expensive. Long flat spans can still fail without a continuous load path. These properties are game balance values, not real-world engineering ratings.

materials.name: Wood Pier
materials.description: A Wood Pier is a low-cost support for lighter loads. Connect its top to a bridge joint so it can carry the load down to the foundation in compression. Taller piers can buckle under less load, so check their stress while the vehicle crosses.

materials.name: Support Rope
materials.description: Support Rope is a light, low-cost way to suspend parts of a deck. Connect the rope to secure supports above the deck so it can carry load when pulled taut. A slack rope provides no support, and a rope cannot carry compression. Each placement adds one rope on each side of the deck.

materials.name: Steel Beam
materials.description: Steel beams resist pulling forces in tension and pushing forces in compression. Connect them in triangles so forces can travel from the road deck through the truss to the supports. Steel Beam costs more per metre than Concrete Beam but adds less weight to the bridge. Each placement adds a matching pair of side beams.

materials.name: Steel Pier
materials.description: The Steel Pier uses a braced frame to carry vertical load in compression. It costs more per metre than the Concrete Pier and adds less weight to the bridge. A taller pier can buckle more easily, so use a sound foundation and brace the bridge where loads enter the pier.

materials.name: Steel Rope
materials.description: A taut steel cable carries tension and transfers load from the deck to towers or anchorages. A slack cable stops supporting the deck, and it cannot carry compression. Use rigid towers or braces for members that must resist pushing forces. Each placement adds a matching cable on either side of the bridge.

materials.name: Wood Road
materials.description: Wood Road gives vehicles a continuous path across the bridge. It is light and inexpensive, which helps keep the bridge's own weight and cost down. Connect each road segment to the next and use beams or piers to carry the load toward the supports.
